prompt.en: A loose reflector falls away from a Yagi, but its driven element and feedline stay intact. Why can the pattern change?

text.en: An unfed element cannot affect radiation, so only the meter calibration can change.

feedback.en: A parasitic element re-radiates coupled energy even without its own feedline.

text.en: The remaining driven element automatically takes over the reflector's length and position.

feedback.en: Its physical dimensions do not change when another element is lost.

text.en: The reflector supplied extra transmitter power, which the array now lacks.

feedback.en: The reflector did not generate power. It helped redistribute coupled energy.

text.en: The coupled parasitic structure has changed, so the original pattern can no longer be assumed.

feedback.en: Element dimensions and positions shape the array pattern. An intact feedline is not enough to preserve it.

explanation.en: Unfed does not mean inactive. Recheck a damaged array rather than trusting its original gain and rear rejection.

prompt.en: Compare an ideal vertical over a symmetric ground system with a Yagi aimed at one station. Which horizontal-pattern contrast fits?

text.en: The vertical is similar in all compass directions; the Yagi concentrates radiation toward its main lobe.

feedback.en: Axial symmetry gives the simple vertical an omnidirectional horizontal pattern; the Yagi is directional.

text.en: Both have the same narrow forward beam because both are resonant.

feedback.en: Resonance does not establish the same radiation pattern.

text.en: The vertical's strongest compass direction follows the coax route.

feedback.en: The ideal symmetric vertical pattern is not steered by coax routing.

text.en: The Yagi is omnidirectional if its SWR is low.

feedback.en: A good impedance match does not erase Yagi directivity.

explanation.en: Impedance match and radiation pattern are separate properties.

prompt.en: Beam A is advertised as 6.7 dBd; beam B as 8.0 dBi under comparable conditions. Which comparison uses a common reference?

text.en: A is lower by 1.3 dB because 6.7 is less than 8.0.

feedback.en: The raw numbers use different references and cannot be subtracted directly.

text.en: A is about 0.8 dB higher because 6.7 dBd is about 8.8 dBi.

feedback.en: Adding the 2.1 dB reference offset puts both on the isotropic scale.

text.en: B is about 3.4 dB higher because dBd must be reduced by 2.1 to get dBi.

feedback.en: That conversion is backwards. A dipole-reference value gains 2.1 when expressed in dBi.

text.en: Both gains are equal because changing the reference changes the antenna pattern.

feedback.en: Reference labels do not change either antenna. These figures still differ after conversion.

explanation.en: Convert gain references before comparing catalogue claims; stacking or extra transmitter power is a separate question.
